label: RM 0006
title: Layered Validation on an Autonomous Path

questions.q: What are DDL and DML, and which of them does the allowlist let through?
questions.a: SQL is taught as one language. It splits into three groups that do very different amounts of damage. DDL changes structure: create, alter, drop, truncate. DML changes rows: insert, update, delete. Reading is select, and it changes nothing. The allowlist permits select and explain, and refuses both of the other groups. What that buys is a precise place to draw the line. “Read-only” stops being an intention and becomes a list a program can check. Worth adding which group really hurts. Drop is loud and immediately noticed. A delete with a slightly wrong predicate is silent, recoverable only from backup, and far more likely to be what a model writes.
questions.flag: Listing drop and truncate as the danger. They are the easy half. The quiet writes are the ones a denylist was never going to catch.

teach.title: The injection claim, corrected

questions.q: What is Snowflake, architecturally?
questions.a: A cloud data warehouse whose defining choice is that storage and compute are pulled apart. The data sits in one place permanently. A warehouse is a compute cluster you size, start and stop independently. Several can read the same tables at once without fighting each other. Access is governed by roles and grants. What that buys is isolation between workloads and a bill you can switch off, because nothing needs to be running for the data to exist. Billing is per second of running compute. That is why a validation step which runs explain, rather than the query itself, is cheap as well as safe.
questions.flag: “It's a cloud database.” The separation of storage and compute is the whole design, and it is what makes the cost argument work.

questions.q: What is SQL injection, and how is it normally prevented?
questions.a: The oldest web vulnerability there is. An application builds a query by gluing user input into a string. A user who types the right punctuation stops being data and becomes syntax. The standard fix is parameter binding. Query text and values are sent to the database separately, so a value can never be reinterpreted as code. What that buys here is nothing, and that is the point worth making. A model writes the entire statement rather than supplying a value to slot into one. There is no parameter to bind. The defence has to be a different shape, which is exactly why the allowlist exists.
questions.flag: Offering parameterised queries as the answer. It is the right answer to a different question, and reaching for it shows you have not thought about this one.

questions.q: What is prompt injection, and why is it the one that matters here?
questions.a: It is text arriving in the model's context that changes what the model does. It does not need to come from a user. A log line, an exception message, a table comment or a column description can all carry instructions. The model has no way to tell data from directions. It matters here because this system reads failures produced by other systems, which is untrusted input by definition. No parser fixes it, and anyone offering one is wrong. The only dependable control is on the far side. Assume the generated statement may be hostile and let nothing but a read through, enforced somewhere the model cannot reach.
questions.flag: Promising to sanitise the input. You cannot sanitise a language model's context. Constrain what its output is allowed to do instead.

questions.q: What is an abstract syntax tree, and what can you prove with one?
questions.a: It is what a parser produces after it has understood your code. The text, the whitespace and the comments are gone. What remains is a tree of typed nodes. An assignment becomes a node with a target and a value, whatever spacing or variable names it was written with. What that buys is checks that survive formatting. A string search for a dangerous call is defeated by a line break, a comment, an alias or a rename. A tree walk is not. You can prove it parses and what shape it has. You cannot prove anything about whether running it is a good idea.
questions.flag: Treating a clean parse as a passing check. It proves the text is Python. It says nothing about whether the fix is right.

teach.title: Layer three: parso, and why not ast

questions.q: Why parso rather than Python's built-in ast?
questions.a: Error recovery. Both turn source into a tree, and they disagree about failure. The standard ast raises on the first syntax error and gives you nothing else. Parso carries on past a broken construct and hands back both a tree and a list of the errors it found. Model-written code is often one broken line among nine good ones. What that buys is seeing all ten problems in one pass instead of one deploy at a time. For a loop that feeds errors back to a model, that is one round trip rather than nine. The cost is that a recovered tree is a guess about what was meant, so a check passing against it is weaker evidence.
questions.flag: Naming the library without naming the property. Nobody chooses a parser for its name, and error recovery is the entire reason.

teach.title: Layer three: parso, and why not ast

questions.q: If every check above it were bypassed, what is left?
questions.a: The database role. Permissions attach to roles, and every connection acts as exactly one role. Least privilege means that role holds only what the job needs. A role with select on four tables and nothing else cannot drop anything, whatever the query text says. The engine refuses before it considers intent. What that buys is defence that does not depend on your own code being correct. Every other layer here is something you wrote and could have got wrong. This one is enforced by the database. If the agent connects as something powerful, your allowlist is the last line, and an allowlist is code you wrote.
questions.flag: Listing application checks and stopping. The interviewer is waiting for the grant, and it is the strongest thing you have.

questions.q: What does “layered validation” actually mean here?
questions.a: Three cheap checks that each rule out a different failure. Schemas in context stop wrong column names being written. EXPLAIN catches anything that does not exist in the warehouse. Parsing catches malformed Python. No single one proves the fix is correct, so they are stacked.
questions.flag: Implying the layers combine into a correctness proof. They rule out classes of wrongness, and saying that is more precise and more honest.

questions.q: What does running EXPLAIN on a generated query prove?
questions.a: That it parses, and that it binds. Every table named exists. Every column exists on the table it is attributed to. The predicate types are compatible. The database's own planner is the authority, so the check cannot drift from reality the way a cached schema file can.
questions.flag: Saying it validates the query. Name the two properties, because the next question is what it does not cover.

teach.title: Layer two: ask the database, do not guess

questions.q: And what does it not prove?
questions.a: Everything about meaning. It does not execute. So it says nothing about the rows returned, or whether the join is the one intended. It says nothing about whether the query finishes in reasonable time. A query can plan perfectly and be completely wrong. That is the honest limit of the layer.
questions.flag: Not having an answer ready. This is the follow-up, every time, and it is the one that shows whether you understood your own guard.

teach.title: Layer two: ask the database, do not guess

questions.q: Why fetch schemas live instead of shipping a schema file?
questions.a: Because a file goes stale and nothing tells you. A column gets renamed and the file does not change. The model then writes a query against a table that no longer looks like that. The tool instead extracts the tables a query references and loads only those. So the context is both current and small.
questions.flag: Missing the selectivity. Loading only the referenced tables is what makes live loading affordable in a warehouse with thousands of them.

teach.title: Layer one: never let it guess a column name

questions.q: How is the injection path actually closed?
questions.a: By an allowlist on statement type. The connector path runs only SELECT and EXPLAIN, so anything else never executes. There is also a keyword denylist covering DROP, DELETE, TRUNCATE, ALTER and CREATE. I would correct my own bullet here, because it names table-name checks and the barrier is the allowlist.
questions.flag: Leading with the denylist. Denylists are the weak half, and leading with the weak half invites exactly the bypass question you do not want.

teach.title: The injection claim, corrected

questions.q: What are the 368 scenarios?
questions.a: Recorded failure cases with ideal answers. Each has an input of code block, error log and type, plus an ideal recommendation with action, investigation, resolution and corrected code. It is an offline evaluation dataset rather than a pytest suite, and I would use the word evaluation rather than regression.
questions.flag: Calling it a test suite. There is a real difference and the interviewer may know it.

teach.title: The 368 scenarios, and what scoring them by similarity means

questions.q: How are those scenarios scored?
questions.a: By semantic similarity. Both the expected and actual text get embedded, the cosine is taken, multiplied by a maximum score and capped. So it measures whether the answer reads like the ideal one. It is a reasonable choice for free-text fields and a weak one for generated code.
questions.flag: Not naming the mechanism. “We score them” is the answer of someone who did not build the harness.

teach.title: The 368 scenarios, and what scoring them by similarity means

questions.q: Where does this validation sit in the debugger's flow?
questions.a: Between the fix being proposed and it being applied. The investigation produces corrected code and validation checks it. Only then can the action router send it to a retrigger. The important caveat is that ENABLE_PIPELINE_VALIDATIONS defaults to false. On a default deployment this layer is not in the path at all.
questions.flag: Describing it as always on. The default says otherwise and config is the first thing a careful interviewer reads.

questions.q: What is the riskiest claim in this bullet?
questions.a: Two of them. “Table-name checks closing the injection path” describes a guard that is documented rather than implemented, and the real barrier is the statement allowlist. And “regression-tested” oversells an offline evaluation set scored by cosine similarity with no threshold reported.
questions.flag: Defending either phrase. The underlying engineering is good, and the wording is what will not survive a careful reader.

teach.title: The injection claim, corrected

questions.q: Distinguish parsing from binding, and say which one matters more here.
questions.a: Parsing is grammar. Binding is resolving names against real schemas. Binding matters more, because a model writing SQL rarely produces ungrammatical SQL. It produces grammatical SQL about a column that does not exist. EXPLAIN is valuable precisely because it reaches the binding stage.
questions.flag: Treating them as the same check. The distinction is why a syntax checker would be nearly useless for the SQL half.

teach.title: Layer three: parso, and why not ast

questions.q: What does the EXPLAIN check cost you?
questions.a: A round trip to Snowflake, on the critical path of an autonomous fix, plus a live connection with credentials. It also means validation fails when the warehouse is unavailable, and you need a decision about what happens then. Failing closed is right for an autonomous path, and it should be explicit.
questions.flag: Calling it free because it does not execute. Planning a query is real work and it is a dependency you have taken on.

questions.q: Give me a concrete case where error recovery changes the outcome.
questions.a: A generated function with two problems. A missing colon on line three and a bad indent on line nine. The ast parser raises on line three and stops, so the feedback names one problem. The model fixes it and resubmits, and only then learns about line nine. parso returns both, so one cycle handles both.
questions.flag: Answering abstractly. A two-error example makes the argument in one sentence.

teach.title: Layer three: parso, and why not ast

questions.q: Why extract tables from the query first rather than load everything?
questions.a: Context budget and signal. A warehouse has thousands of tables, and their combined schema does not fit in a prompt. Even if it did, burying the five relevant tables among thousands makes the model's job harder. Extracting first means the context is exactly the definitions that matter.
questions.flag: Only citing token cost. The signal argument is the stronger half and most people miss it.

teach.title: Layer one: never let it guess a column name

questions.q: Why is an allowlist stronger than a denylist here?
questions.a: Because a denylist protects against what you remembered. The keyword list covers five statements and a substring test over upper-cased text has obvious gaps. An allowlist permitting only SELECT and EXPLAIN refuses everything nobody thought of, which is the class that actually hurts you.
questions.flag: Presenting the denylist as the control. It is defence in depth behind the real barrier, and the ordering matters when you describe it.

teach.title: The injection claim, corrected

questions.q: The bullet mentions import and runtime checks. Where do those live?
questions.a: In the pytest suite around the validation framework, not in validate_python_code. That function parses and reports syntax errors. The test suite covers syntax, indentation, import and runtime error cases as scenarios. I would separate those two things rather than let the bullet imply one function does all four.
questions.flag: Letting the list stand as one pipeline. Two mechanisms are being described, and only one of them runs before a fix is applied.

teach.title: Layer three: parso, and why not ast

questions.q: Why score by semantic similarity at all?
questions.a: Because most of the output is free text. An investigation and a resolution are prose, and there is no exact match to test against. Embedding both and taking a cosine is a defensible way to score prose at scale. It is the right tool for those fields, and the wrong one for the code field.
questions.flag: Dismissing it. It is a reasonable choice, and the interesting answer is where it stops being reasonable.

teach.title: The 368 scenarios, and what scoring them by similarity means

questions.q: What does cosine similarity actually reward?
questions.a: Reading like the ideal answer. Two correct investigations phrased differently can score poorly. A confident, fluent, wrong investigation using the right vocabulary can score well. So the metric is measuring register as much as correctness, and that gap is worth stating before someone else finds it.
questions.flag: Saying it measures semantic correctness. It measures semantic proximity, and proximity to a right answer is not the same as being right.

teach.title: The 368 scenarios, and what scoring them by similarity means

questions.q: You score corrected code by similarity. What would you do instead?
questions.a: Run it through the oracle I already have. For SQL, EXPLAIN the generated fix against the same schema and score binary validity. For Python, parse it. That turns the code field from a fuzzy match into a deterministic check, using machinery already written for the live path.
questions.flag: Not connecting the two halves of the chapter. The eval harness ignores a validator the production path already uses, and noticing that is the point of the question.

questions.q: The harness reports a pass rate. Passing what?
questions.a: That is the gap I would flag. EvalSummary carries passed, failed and error case counts plus a pass rate and an average score, so a threshold exists somewhere in the runner. What is not in the documentation is what that threshold is, what it gates, or any recorded score. Without those, it is a harness rather than a gate.
questions.flag: Quoting a pass rate you cannot source. If you do not have the number, say the harness exists and the number was not published.

teach.title: The 368 scenarios, and what scoring them by similarity means

questions.q: What layer is missing?
questions.a: A blast-radius check. Every current layer asks whether the fix is well-formed. None asks how much it would change. A generated UPDATE touching ten rows and one touching ten million both pass every check here. Counting affected rows before applying is the layer I would add, and it is the one that maps to actual damage.
questions.flag: Proposing more of the same. Another syntax-level check adds nothing. The missing axis is magnitude, not correctness.

questions.q: Give me a fix that passes every layer and is still dangerous.
questions.a: An UPDATE with a predicate that is valid but too broad. It parses, it binds, every column exists, and it changes ten million rows instead of ten. Nothing in this stack measures magnitude. That is the gap, and the missing layer is a row-count estimate before applying.
questions.flag: Reaching for an exotic example. The boring over-broad predicate is the realistic one and it makes the point better.

teach.title: Layer two: ask the database, do not guess

questions.q: Snowflake is unreachable when a fix needs validating.
questions.a: The SQL layer cannot run, and the decision is which way it fails. On an autonomous path it has to fail closed. An unvalidated fix is then never applied. Failing open would mean the one time validation mattered most is the time it was skipped. That is the worst possible correlation.
questions.flag: Suggesting a cached schema fallback. That reintroduces the staleness problem live loading exists to solve.

teach.title: Layer one: never let it guess a column name

questions.q: Python that parses cleanly but fails immediately on import.
questions.a: Passes the parse layer, because parsing is grammar. A missing module or a bad name is a runtime concern and parso never resolves names. The bullet's mention of import checks comes from the pytest suite rather than from this validator. Closing it properly means importing in a sandbox, which is a bigger commitment.
questions.flag: Claiming the parser catches imports. It is a structural check and imports are a resolution-time concern.

teach.title: Layer three: parso, and why not ast

questions.q: The schema changes between validation and the retrigger.
questions.a: Then the fix was validated against a warehouse that no longer exists in that shape. It is a time-of-check to time-of-use gap. During a migration that is real rather than theoretical. The window is small, and the mitigation is to validate as late as possible. Validate immediately before applying, not at proposal time.
questions.flag: Dismissing it as unlikely. Naming it as a TOCTOU gap shows you recognised the pattern, which is the whole point.

questions.q: How would you get a destructive statement past the keyword denylist?
questions.a: Several ways, which is the argument against denylists. Comments inside a keyword, a statement type nobody listed, or something reached through a stored procedure. I would not lean on it. The control that holds is the allowlist, because a statement that is not a SELECT or an EXPLAIN never reaches the connector at all.
questions.flag: Defending the denylist as sufficient. It is not, you already have something better, and saying so is the strong answer.

teach.title: The injection claim, corrected

questions.q: The 368 scenarios were recorded once. What happens as the platform changes?
questions.a: They age, and a stale case is worse than no case. Ideal answers referencing tables that were since renamed will fail a correct system, and passing them becomes a regression. Any fixed evaluation set needs an owner and a refresh cadence, and neither is documented here.
questions.flag: Treating a recorded dataset as permanent. It is a snapshot of a moving system.

teach.title: The 368 scenarios, and what scoring them by similarity means

questions.q: You find out validation was off in production the whole time. What do you say?
questions.a: That the flag defaults to false and I should have checked which way it was set. Then the useful part. The layers still constrained the model during development. The statement allowlist is a separate control and it is always on. So the destructive path was closed even with validation off, and the correctness checks were not.
questions.flag: Getting defensive. Separating which protections were live from which were not is the answer that rebuilds credibility.

teach.title: The injection claim, corrected

questions.q: What would you change, in order?
questions.a: Turn the validation flag on and require it before any autonomous apply. Score the corrected-code field with the validator instead of a cosine, since the oracle already exists. Add a row-count estimate as a blast-radius check. Then publish a threshold so the harness becomes a gate rather than a report.
questions.flag: Listing them without an order. The ordering is the judgment, and the first one is a config change with the largest payoff.

teach.title: The 368 scenarios, and what scoring them by similarity means

questions.q: A generated SQL fix passes the EXPLAIN check. What has that established?
questions.a:
Parsing and binding. The planner resolved every table and column against the real warehouse and the predicate types were compatible. That rules out a large class of errors in one round trip, and it never executes the query.

It establishes nothing about meaning. A query can plan perfectly and return the wrong rows, join the wrong way, or scan a table for an hour. What stops a destructive statement is a different control entirely: the allowlist that permits only SELECT and EXPLAIN.
options: That it parses and binds against the live schema
That it returns the rows the author actually wanted
That it runs faster than the query being checked
That it cannot drop or alter any existing table

teach.title: Layer two: ask the database, do not guess

questions.q: How does the 368-scenario suite decide whether an answer was good?
questions.a:
Embeddings and a cosine, multiplied by a maximum score and capped. That is a sensible way to score prose fields like an investigation, where no exact match exists.

The last option is the interesting wrong answer, because it is what the harness should do for the corrected-code field. The production path already has an oracle for that: run EXPLAIN on the generated SQL. Scoring code by how similar it reads is the weakest part of this evaluation.
options: Cosine similarity between embeddings of expected and actual
An identical string comparison against the stored answer
A separate model adjudicating whether the answer holds
Whether the corrected code executed without raising errors

teach.title: The 368 scenarios, and what scoring them by similarity means

questions.q: “What does EXPLAIN actually prove?”
questions.a: Two things: the query parses, and it binds. Every table exists, every column exists on the table it is attributed to, and the predicate types are compatible. The planner is the authority so the check cannot go stale. It proves nothing about meaning, because it never runs. A query can plan perfectly and return entirely the wrong rows, and that is the honest limit of the layer.

teach.title: Layer two: ask the database, do not guess

questions.q: “Can a fix pass all your checks and still break production?”
questions.a: Yes, and the realistic case is an over-broad predicate. A statement that parses, binds and touches ten million rows instead of ten passes every layer here, because every layer asks whether the fix is well-formed and none asks how much it changes. The missing layer is blast radius: estimate affected rows before applying. That is the one I would add next.

questions.q: “How do you prevent SQL injection?”
questions.a: The barrier is an allowlist: the connector path executes only SELECT and EXPLAIN, so anything else never runs whatever it contains. Behind that there is a keyword denylist for DROP, DELETE, TRUNCATE, ALTER and CREATE, and I would not rely on that half, because a denylist only covers what somebody remembered. I would also correct my own bullet, which names table-name checks.

teach.title: The injection claim, corrected

questions.q: “Your evaluation scores generated code by similarity. Is that sound?”
questions.a: For the prose fields it is defensible, since an investigation has no exact match to test against. For the corrected-code field it is the weakest part of the harness. We already have an oracle on the production path: EXPLAIN for SQL and a parse for Python. Scoring the code field with the validator instead of a cosine would make that part deterministic, and it is reusing code that already exists.

teach.title: The 368 scenarios, and what scoring them by similarity means

questions.q: “Was this validation actually on?”
questions.a: ENABLE_PIPELINE_VALIDATIONS defaults to false, so on a default deployment the layer is not in the path. That is the ship-dark pattern and it is a reasonable way to introduce a check that can block work, but leaving it there is not. Worth separating what was still live: the statement allowlist is an independent control and it is always on, so the destructive path stayed closed even with validation off.
